# A Map of AI-for-Architecture Work {#sec-appendix-b-ai-for-architecture-map}

```{=latex}
\abstract*{This appendix consolidates the prior body of AI-for-architecture work that Architecture 2.0 builds on. It groups established results into families, maps each family to the architecture capabilities it most advances and to the chapter that develops it, and states how the discipline in this book differs from any single family. The map is a reading aid and a positioning statement, not a survey.}
```

Machine learning has appeared in computer architecture for decades, first inside shipped mechanisms and later as tool-using systems that participate in the design process itself. The families below are the strands this material draws on. Collecting them serves a narrow purpose. It is not another survey, which existing work already provides [@ChenPenneyJimenez2020AIArchitecture], but a positioning aid that shows what each family contributes, which of the six architecture capabilities it most advances, and where this book puts it to use (@tbl-ai-arch-map).

The rows fall into three regimes, and the regime determines what a result can claim. In the first, learning ships inside the mechanism and is judged by the mechanism's own budget, a mispredict rate at a fixed area. In the second, learning models the design space and is judged by predictive fidelity against the tool it replaces. In the third, learning participates in the design process itself, and the unit of judgment shifts from the artifact to the loop, which is where this book lives. Confusing the regimes is how a shipped branch predictor gets cited as evidence that an agent can be trusted with a floorplan.

| **Family of work** | **Representative results** | **Capabilities advanced** | **Developed in** | **Key sources** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Learned in-chip components** | Perceptron branch predictors and research-stage learned prefetchers, where learning is embedded in the mechanism itself and does a bounded tactical job | Implement, Evaluate | @sec-moonshot, @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization | [@JimenezLin2001Perceptron; @ChenPenneyJimenez2020AIArchitecture] |
| **Learned cost models and predictive DSE** | Surrogates and regression models that predict performance and power across a design space from cheap features | Explore, Evaluate | @sec-data-representations-world-models, @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization | [@IpekEtAl2006PredictiveDSE; @LeeBrooks2006RegressionModeling; @BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer] |
| **Autotuning and autoschedulers** | Statistical search over compiler and tensor-program schedules guided by measured hardware | Explore | @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization | [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM; @ZhengEtAl2020Ansor; @RaganKelleyEtAl2017HalideCACM] |
| **Hardware-software co-design and joint search** | Joint search over accelerator hardware and the software mapped onto it, co-optimizing the pair rather than either alone | Explore, Implement | @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales, @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack | [@yazdanbakhsh2021apollo; @HongEtAl2023DOSA] |
| **RL for physical design, datapath, and flow tuning** | Reinforcement learning for macro placement and datapath synthesis, and commercial design-space tools | Explore, Implement | @sec-architecture-20-ontology, @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack, @sec-what-architect-owns | [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement; @RoyEtAl2021PrefixRL; @Synopsys2023DSOai] |
| **LLMs for RTL and HLS generation** | Natural-language and high-level input lowered toward RTL, extending the high-level-synthesis lineage | Formulate, Implement | @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces, @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization | [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo; @ThakurEtAl2023VeriGen; @ThakurEtAl2023AutoChip; @CoussyMorawiec2008HighLevelSynthesis; @FuEtAl2023GPT4AIGChip] |
| **Agentic, tool-using exploration** | Agents that propose candidates, call tools, read the returned results, and revise a search | Formulate through Defend | @sec-architecture-20-ontology, @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces, @sec-running-the-loop | [@WangEtAl2026AgentDSE; @KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym] |
| **Benchmarks and datasets** | Datasets and question sets that test architectural understanding and reasoning | Evaluate, Explain | @sec-data-representations-world-models, @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect | [@PrakashEtAl2025QuArch] |
| **ML for verification and validation** | Coverage-directed test generation, and LLM-drafted assertions and testbenches that verification engineers once wrote by hand | Evaluate, Defend | @sec-feedback-verification-trust | [@FangEtAl2025AssertLLM; @QiuEtAl2024AutoBench; @KangEtAl2024FVEval] |

: **The unit of work in Architecture 2.0 is the bounded study and its reviewable claim, not any single family's artifact:** each row names the prior results, the architecture capabilities the family most advances, and the chapters that develop it. The capabilities column uses the six lifecycle verbs, and the region each family occupies in the book's composition map is walked in the prose that follows. {#tbl-ai-arch-map tbl-colwidths="[20,28,15,22,15]"}

These families are not exclusive. An agentic design-space search may call a learned cost model, invoke an autoscheduler, and emit RTL, meaning a single study can touch several rows at once.

The learned in-chip components family carries a filter the others do not. A learned component reaches silicon only when its inference pays for itself inside the mechanism's own budget, a prediction delivered within the cycle, from tables measured in kilobytes, at microwatts. The perceptron predictor cleared that bar and reached commercial cores; the neural prefetchers of the research literature have not, because hiding a miss is worthless if the machinery that hides it costs more than the miss. Every proposal in that family gets checked against that arithmetic before anything else.

The families also occupy distinct regions of the territory drawn in @fig-book-composition. The learned-components, cost-model, autotuning, and co-design families live where architecture meets ML. Reinforcement learning for physical design and LLM-driven RTL generation live where ML meets EDA, alongside the older learned analysis surrogates that predicted routability hotspots from placement features, estimated IR drop without a full power-grid solve, and flagged lithography hotspots before mask synthesis, all inside production tools years before reinforcement learning placed a macro [@Kahng2018Machine]. Those surrogates are the cost-model family transplanted into physical design, a cheap learned stand-in for an analysis too slow to sit inside the iteration loop, and they are worth remembering when judging what ML in EDA has already proven versus what it still promises. Verification and validation span both regions, since coverage-directed test generation and machine-drafted assertions produce the evidence an architect brings to signoff. Only the agentic, tool-using family, together with the benchmarks that evaluate it, reaches toward the center, the loop that must cross all three fields.

Reading down the capabilities column shows a related asymmetry. Prior work clusters in Explore, Implement, and Evaluate, while Explain and Defend stay thinly populated, worked mainly by the agentic, benchmark, and verification families. That thin territory is what this book develops.

Because these methods often combine, what separates Architecture 2.0 from any single family is its unit of work. A learned branch predictor improves one mechanism. A macro-placement agent improves one implementation step. An RTL-generating model produces one artifact. Each is valuable, and each is judged on its own narrow output.

This material instead takes the bounded study and its reviewable claim as the unit. The question is not just whether a model produced a plausible artifact, but whether the whole loop—from intent through tools to evidence—supports an architectural decision that another architect can inspect and challenge. The families mapped here supply the methods; the discipline supplies the standard of judgment that decides what their outputs are worth.

## Candidates, Not Decisions

Those outputs are always candidates, not decisions. A learned model, an autoscheduler, or an agentic search proposes a macro placement or an RTL block, but that candidate first has to pass functional verification, then clear the physical-design flow against power, area, timing closure, and routing congestion before it counts. The methods explore the space; the architect owns signoff, which spans functional, timing, power, and physical checks. Verification is also where a machine that writes its own tests can fool itself, because a generated assertion suite can pass vacuously while checking nothing that matters (@sec-feedback-verification-trust). This division of labor is the constant the rest of the book returns to. When assessing RL agents like AlphaChip, the total cost must include pre-training the full policy-and-value network, its graph encoder included, before the agent ever proposes a layout for the target chip [@ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement].
